title: Accessing Few-Layer CrI$_3$ Magnetoelasticity Through Bulk Single Crystals
authors: J. Arneth, M. Möller, D. A. S. Kaib, P. P. Stavropoulos, A. Razpopov, M. Jonak, S. Spachmann, M. Abdel-Hafiez, S. Biswas, K. Riedl, R. Valentí, R. Klingeler
abstract: The persistence of ferromagnetic long-range order in monolayers of the van der Waals semiconductor CrI$_3$ opens new routes for spintronic applications based on two-dimensional quantum magnets. In the fabrication of such devices, the constituent materials inevitably experience anisotropic strain, which modifies their intrinsic electronic properties. At the same time, strain can serve as a powerful tuning parameter, driving the material to desired regimes. While several theoretical studies have investigated the effect of biaxial in-plane strain on CrI$_3$ numerically, experiments are widely limited to the application of hydrostatic pressure. Here, we perform high-resolution magnetostriction experiments on bulk CrI$_3$ samples, and \textit{ab-initio}-based magnetoelastic calculations, to elucidate the role of uniaxial lattice strain on the magnetic properties. Our data show that magnetostriction in CrI$_3$ is unexpectedly sensitive to surface effects, which enables us to investigate the influence of in-plane and out-of-plane strain separately, in both the bulk ferromagnetic (BFM) phase emerging at $T_{\rm C}=61\,\mathrm{K}$ and the surface antiferromagnetic (SAFM) phase below $T^* \simeq 50\,\mathrm{K}$. In particular, we quantify the uniaxial strain dependence of the surface interlayer coupling $J^{\rm SAFM}_{\perp}$ and the surface spin-flip field $B^*$, which drastically exceed the strain effects in the BFM phase by a factor of $\sim 30$. The large magnetostrictive response allows us to study the magnetoelastic coupling in few-layer CrI$_3$ through experiments on bulk single crystals, without requiring exfoliation.
summary: This work investigates how uniaxial strain affects the magnetism of few-layer $	ext{CrI}_3$ by combining magnetostriction experiments on bulk crystals with theoretical calculations. The key finding is that surface effects dominate the magnetoelastic response, allowing researchers to study crucial magnetic couplings in both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases using readily available single crystals.
main_problem: To elucidate the role of uniaxial lattice strain on the magnetic properties and magnetoelastic coupling in few-layer $	ext{CrI}_3$ without requiring material exfoliation.
main_result: Magnetostriction is highly sensitive to surface effects, allowing separate investigation of in-plane and out-of-plane strain. The surface antiferromagnetic (SAFM) phase exhibits magnetostrictive responses significantly larger than those in the bulk ferromagnetic (BFM) phase.
method: The study combines high-resolution magnetostriction experiments on bulk single crystals with ab-initio magnetoelastic calculations using first-principles methods.
model_or_system: The physical system is the van der Waals semiconductor $	ext{CrI}_3$, which exhibits distinct BFM and SAFM magnetic phases. The analysis models the interplay between strain, magnetism, and surface/bulk contributions to the overall material properties.
key_observables: Magnetostriction ($	ext{d}L/	ext{L}$), magnetization ($M$), uniaxial strain dependence of interlayer coupling ($J^{m SAFM}_{\perp}$), and spin-flip field ($B^*$).
important_parameters: Critical temperatures ($T_{m C}=61\,\mathrm{K}$, $T^* \simeq 50\,\mathrm{K}$), strain magnitude, and the ratio of surface to bulk contributions.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that magnetostriction measurements can effectively probe directional strain effects, overcoming historical limitations to hydrostatic pressure only.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows measured isothermal magnetostriction ($	ext{d}L/	ext{L}$) and corresponding magnetization ($M$) curves for both $B \parallel c$ and $B \parallel ab$.
paper_structure: The paper structure moves from establishing the potential of $	ext{CrI}_3$ for spintronics to presenting experimental magnetostriction data, followed by theoretical calculations that separate strain effects in the BFM and SAFM phases.
why_interesting: The detailed study of magnetoelastic coupling using measurable bulk properties (magnetostriction) provides an accessible route to probe quantum magnetic phenomena typically restricted to highly controlled 2D systems or high-pressure environments, which is relevant for understanding emergent quantum states in layered materials.

FIG. 2. Isothermal magnetostriction (blue) and differential magnetic susceptibility (orange) for B ∥c (a) and B ∥ab (b) at T = 2 K. Vertical dashed lines mark characteristic magnetic fieldsa, as described in the text. Sketches illustrate the Cr3+ spin structure in the corresponding field ranges. Closed (open) circles mark up-(down-)sweeps of the magnetic field.

FIG. 3. Magnetic phase diagrams obtained from dilatometry (black data points) and magnetization (blue data points) mea- surements for B ∥c (a) and B ∥ab (b). PM, FM, SPM+BFM and SAFM+BFM label paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, mixed surface paramagnetic and bulk ferromagnetic, and mixed surface antiferromagnetic and bulk ferromagnetic phases, respectively. In (a), a hysteresis region is denoted by the striped region around B∗. Green shaded areas depict field regimes where the BFM phase is not fully polarized. Data points marking the PM-FM-crossover were obtained by ac susceptibility measurements (see the Appendix for more details). All lines serve as guides to the eye.

FIG. 4. Low-temperature Cr site honeycomb network in CrI3 for (a) the layers proximate to the surface (with C2/m symmetry) and (b) the bulk (with R¯3 symmetry). The intralayer nearest neighbors X-, Y- and Z-bonds are show in blue, red, and green respectively. The interlayer bonds are labeled JSAFM ⊥ and JBFM ⊥ . Each layer consists of 8-sites, representing the cluster used within the SCCMFT calculations.
